8.4.4 DIGESTIVE SYSTEM OF FROG
Let’s discuss given questions. i. What is the digestive system? ii. What are the end products of carbohydrate, protein and fat digestion? iii. What is the feeding habit of frog?

Digestion is the process of conversion of complex food particles into simpler forms. For this, various organs are co-ordinating or working together called digestive organs forming a complex system called digestive system. Mainly two processes involve in the process of digestion which are mechanical and chemical. Mechanical process is the conversion of larger food particles into smaller or fine state whereas chemical pocess is the conversion of complex organic compound in food into simpler forms. Digestive system in frog can be discussed under two headings: A. ALIMENTARY CANAL In frog, alimentary canal is a complete, long and coiled tube of varying diameter extending from mouth to cloaca. Alimentary canal includes the mouth, buccal cavity, pharynx, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine and cloaca.

Figure 8.4.7 Mouth open to show the parts of buccal cavity 1. Mouth: The alimentary canal starts with a wide opening called mouth. It is a transverse gape bounded by upper and lower jaws covered by immovable lips. Upper jaw is immovable but lower jaw is partially movable which can be moved up and down for closing and opening mouth respectively.

2. Bucco-pharyngeal Cavity: Mouth posteriorly leads into a wide and spacious cavity called oral cavity or buccal cavity. In frog, due to the absence of neck, its buccal cavity and pharynx are not distinct and hence called bucco-pharyngeal cavity. Buccopharyngeal cavity serves as the common passage of food and air. Posterior part of buccal cavity is often called as pharynx. The bucco-pharyngeal cavity is internally lined by ciliated columnar epithelium with mucus secreting cells or goblet cells. The function of mucus is to lubricate the food particles for swallowing easily. There are no salivary glands. Structures present in bucco-pharyngeal cavity are:

i. Teeth: The upper jaw is provided with a row of closely set, small, conical and backwardly pointed teeth over the premaxillae and maxillae bones. Teeth on premaxilla and maxilla are called premaxillary and maxillary teeth respectively. The lower jaw does not bear teeth. Besides, there are two more patches of teeth, each patch lying on the either side of the median line of the roof of the buccal cavity called vomerine teeth.
